title: One Bhagat a day
hookLine: a week of reading a different Bhagat each morning

lines: A WEEK BACK, A WEEK AHEAD.
cards: Seven sticky notes on the bathroom mirror. Each has a name and a page number in marker: Ramanand. Bhikhan.
Jaidev. Farid. A week of mornings, one voice per morning, before the phone gets a turn.
Today does two jobs: it looks back at this week's voices, and it hands over a small plan for the next seven. One Bhagat a day.

teach.h: A WEEK OF VOICES, LOOKED BACK ON.
teach.b: First, the week behind us. Satta and Balvand, the minstrels whose Var, tradition says, was sung after a quarrel was forgiven. The saloks headed with Mardana's name, words to a friend.
Sundar's Sadd: Guru Amar Das asking for singing, not weeping. The Gurus answering voices they would put differently, rather than erasing them. The Bhagats' trades, reading like a whole street.
And yesterday, all of it sung as gurbani. Now the week ahead. The Granth is long, and a reader can stand at the front of it and not know where to begin, so here's a doorway the size of a morning.
The ang, the page number, is the address. Day one, Ramanand in Raag Basant, Ang 1195: a home colored with love. Day two, Bhikhan in Sorath, Ang 659: the Name as medicine.
Day three, Jaidev in Gujri, Ang 526, the old poet. Day four, Farid in Asa, Ang 488: the heart and the lips. Day five, Parmanand and Surdas, side by side on Ang 1253.
Day six, Ravidas in Gauri, Ang 345, and the city without sorrow he calls Begampura.
Day seven, a handful of Kabir's saloks, near the end of the book. Each reading is short; some are a few lines.
Read it slowly, once, in Gurmukhi if you can, in a translation if you can't.
Then stop. The point isn't covering ground. It's sitting with one voice long enough to hear how it speaks: Farid's longing, Kabir's sharp edge, Ravidas's dream of a city.
By the end of the week, the names stop being a list and become people.

how: Some Sikhs read from the Granth each day, and some keep a sehaj path, a slow reading of the whole Granth over time; a reader may also return to favorite shabads by their ang number.

o: a chapter grouped by one author
a short prayer said at dawn
a page of the Guru Granth Sahib

games.q: the week ahead — tap the pairs.

s: the point of one a day is to cover as much of the Granth as possible
the point is to sit with one voice long enough to hear how it speaks.
Parmanand and Surdas appear on the same ang
both are on Ang 1253, in Raag Sarang.
the ang is the page number, so it works as an address
a reader can find any of these hymns by its ang.

games.q: it's morning, the Granth is open to a Bhagat's hymn, and you have five minutes. what do you do?
o: read as many hymns as you can before time runs out.
read one hymn slowly, once, and stop.
save it for a free weekend.
games.why: the plan is one voice a day, read slowly, so the names become people rather than a list.

practice: If you can, open to one of those angs now, read a few lines slowly, and close it before the sit.

If not, hold Ramanand's line in your own words, why go out looking, when home is colored with love, and breathe with it; if you pray, Waheguru can ride each breath out. When the to-do list pulls at you, let the line call you back.
